questions.stem: The SI (Système International) has how many BASE UNITS?

options.option_text: SEVEN

questions.explanation: THE SEVEN SI BASE UNITS (rebased in 2019 on physical constants): | Quantity | Unit | Symbol | (1) LENGTH = metre (m); (2) MASS = kilogram (kg); (3) TIME = second (s); (4) ELECTRIC CURRENT = ampere (A); (5) TEMPERATURE = kelvin (K); (6) AMOUNT OF SUBSTANCE = mole (mol); (7) LUMINOUS INTENSITY = candela (cd). MNEMONIC: 'Some Kids Must Sail Around To Canada' (S-K-M-S-A-T-C → s, kg, m, s, A, T→K, cd) or 'MKS A K mol cd'. 2019 REDEFINITION: on 20 May 2019 (World Metrology Day), all 7 SI base units were redefined in terms of 7 PHYSICAL CONSTANTS (fixed exact values): (a) Caesium frequency Δνₛ Cs (second); (b) Speed of light c (metre); (c) Planck constant h (kilogram — replaced the last physical artifact, the Sèvres cylinder!); (d) Elementary charge e (ampere); (e) Boltzmann constant k (kelvin); (f) Avogadro number NA (mole); (g) Luminous efficacy Kcd (candela). KILOGRAM was the LAST base unit tied to a physical artefact (IPK — International Prototype of the Kilogram, a 1889 platinum-iridium cylinder in Sèvres, Paris); now defined by Planck's constant via the Kibble balance. SI also has 2 SUPPLEMENTARY units (dimensionless): RADIAN (plane angle) + STERADIAN (solid angle) — now classified as derived. metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela.

questions.stem: The SI unit of FORCE is:

options.option_text: Joule (J)
NEWTON (N) = kg·m/s² — force required to accelerate a 1 kg mass by 1 m/s²
Watt (W)
Pascal (Pa)

questions.explanation: NEWTON (N) — SI UNIT of FORCE, named after SIR ISAAC NEWTON. DEFINITION: 1 N = force needed to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s². Dimensional formula: [M L T⁻²]. EXAMPLES: a 100-gram apple weighs ~1 N on Earth (mg = 0.1 × 9.8 ≈ 0.98 N); a 10 kg mass weighs ~98 N; an adult's body weight (70 kg) ≈ 686 N. KEY DERIVED SI UNITS: (1) JOULE (J) = N·m = kg·m²/s² → ENERGY / WORK (James Prescott Joule). (2) WATT (W) = J/s → POWER (James Watt); 1 horsepower ≈ 746 W. (3) PASCAL (Pa) = N/m² → PRESSURE (Blaise Pascal); atmospheric pressure ~101325 Pa = 1.013 bar = 760 mmHg. (4) HERTZ (Hz) = s⁻¹ → FREQUENCY (Heinrich Hertz). (5) COULOMB (C) = A·s → ELECTRIC CHARGE. (6) VOLT (V) = W/A = J/C → ELECTRIC POTENTIAL. (7) OHM (Ω) = V/A → RESISTANCE. (8) FARAD (F) = C/V → CAPACITANCE. (9) TESLA (T) = Wb/m² → MAGNETIC FLUX DENSITY. (10) WEBER (Wb) = V·s → MAGNETIC FLUX. (11) LUMEN (lm), LUX (lx) → LIGHT. (12) BECQUEREL (Bq), GRAY (Gy), SIEVERT (Sv) → RADIOACTIVITY. All named SI derived units are named after SCIENTISTS. Dyne (CGS) = 10⁻⁵ N; pound-force (Imperial) ≈ 4.448 N.

questions.stem: The SI unit of ELECTRIC CURRENT is the AMPERE (A). After the 2019 redefinition, one ampere is defined in terms of:

options.option_text: Flow between two parallel wires
The FIXED VALUE of the ELEMENTARY CHARGE e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 1 A = flow of (1/e) elementary charges per second
Mass of copper deposited in electrolysis
Faraday's constant

questions.explanation: AMPERE (A) — SI UNIT of ELECTRIC CURRENT, named after ANDRÉ-MARIE AMPÈRE. 2019 REDEFINITION (20 May 2019): The ampere is defined by taking the FIXED NUMERICAL VALUE of the ELEMENTARY CHARGE e to be exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (coulomb), where the coulomb = A·s. So 1 AMPERE = flow of 1/(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) = ~6.2415 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges per second. OLD (pre-2019) DEFINITION: 'that constant current which, when maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length + negligible cross-section, placed 1 metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length between them' (based on Ampere's force law). The old definition tied ampere to μ₀ (permeability of free space, exact by definition = 4π × 10⁻⁷). NEW definition frees μ₀ to be a measured quantity. OHM'S LAW: V = IR. 1 A is a SIGNIFICANT current — lethal through heart can be as low as 50 mA; household mains fuse at 6/16/32 A; 1000 A is industrial welding scale; lightning bolt can carry 30,000 A. MILLIAMPERE (mA) = 10⁻³ A; MICROAMPERE (µA) = 10⁻⁶ A.

questions.stem: The SI unit of PRESSURE is:

options.option_text: Newton (N)
PASCAL (Pa) = N/m²
Bar
Torr

questions.explanation: PASCAL (Pa) — SI unit of PRESSURE + STRESS. 1 Pa = 1 N/m² = 1 kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². NAMED after BLAISE PASCAL (1623-1662), French mathematician/physicist. PASCAL IS A SMALL UNIT — atmospheric pressure at sea level ≈ 1,01,325 Pa = 101.325 kPa = 1.013 bar. Common pressure multiples: kilopascal (kPa = 10³ Pa), megapascal (MPa = 10⁶ Pa), gigapascal (GPa = 10⁹ Pa — material strengths). OTHER PRESSURE UNITS: (1) BAR = 10⁵ Pa (meteorology + industry); millibar (mb) = 100 Pa = 1 hPa (weather maps). (2) ATMOSPHERE (atm) = 101,325 Pa. (3) TORR = 1/760 atm ≈ 133.3 Pa (vacuum). (4) mmHg = 1 Torr (blood pressure, barometers — normal BP 120/80 mmHg = 16/10.7 kPa). (5) PSI (pound per square inch) ≈ 6,895 Pa (tire pressure, US industry; car tire ~30 psi). BOYLE'S LAW: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (isothermal). PASCAL'S LAW: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions (hydraulic press, brake). ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced. At Mt Everest summit (8,848m), atm pressure drops to ~33% of sea-level value — why climbers need oxygen. Mariana Trench bottom (~11 km) pressure ~1,100 atm.

questions.stem: One LIGHT-YEAR is approximately equal to:

options.option_text: One trillion kilometres
9.461 × 10¹² km ≈ 9.46 TRILLION KILOMETRES
365 million km
Same as 1 astronomical unit

questions.explanation: LIGHT-YEAR (ly) — DISTANCE (not time!) that light travels in one Julian year in vacuum. CALCULATION: speed of light c = 299,792,458 m/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; seconds in a year = 365.25 × 24 × 3600 = 31,557,600 s; distance = c × t ≈ 9.461 × 10¹⁵ m = 9,461,000,000,000 km ≈ 9.46 TRILLION km ≈ 5.88 trillion miles. EXAMPLES: (a) Sun is ~8.3 LIGHT-MINUTES from Earth (not years). (b) PROXIMA CENTAURI (nearest star to the Sun) is 4.24 ly. (c) MILKY WAY galaxy diameter ~100,000 ly. (d) ANDROMEDA GALAXY (M31) ~2.5 million ly. (e) Observable universe diameter ~93 BILLION ly. OTHER ASTRONOMICAL DISTANCES: (1) ASTRONOMICAL UNIT (AU) = mean Earth-Sun distance = 149,597,870,700 m ≈ 150 million km. 1 ly ≈ 63,241 AU. (2) PARSEC (pc) = 3.26 ly ≈ 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m — distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond; used in professional astronomy. 1 kiloparsec (kpc), 1 megaparsec (Mpc). (3) LIGHT-YEAR vs CENTURY in popular media: confusingly used 'I'll wait a light-year' is wrong — light-year is distance. HUBBLE CONSTANT: ~70 km/s/Mpc — measures rate of universe's expansion. REDSHIFT is how distant galaxies are measured. distance light travels in 1 year in vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.stem: HORSEPOWER (1 HP, the unit used for engines) equals approximately:

options.option_text: 1 kilowatt exactly

questions.explanation: HORSEPOWER (HP) — originally defined by JAMES WATT in the 1780s as a way to market his improved steam engines to replace horses. He estimated a pit pony could lift 22,000 foot-pounds/min; multiplied by 1.5 to be safe → 33,000 foot-pounds/min = 550 foot-pounds/sec = 746 W (mechanical HP). VARIANTS: (1) MECHANICAL HP (imperial) = 745.70 W — US + UK engine ratings; (2) METRIC HP (PS / CV / cheval vapeur) = 735.5 W — continental Europe, India, Japan; (3) Electrical HP = 746 W exactly (used for electric motor ratings). DIFFERENCE: manufacturer spec sheets: a car rated 100 PS (metric) = 98.6 HP (mechanical); significant for marketing. EXAMPLES: (a) Peak human sprint ~1.2 HP briefly; sustained cycling ~0.1 HP. (b) Honda Activa ~8 HP; Maruti Alto ~67 HP; Toyota Fortuner ~200 HP; F1 car ~1000 HP. (c) Boeing 777 engine ~100,000 HP each. (d) 1 HP air-conditioner = 1 TON cooling in loose Indian usage (technically 1 ton refrigeration = 3.517 kW = 4.71 HP — i.e., '1 Ton AC' ≈ 3.5 kW, but 'horsepower rating' on inverters uses diff scale). SI UNIT: WATT (W) is the proper SI unit of power; 1 kW = 1000 W. 1 kWh (kilowatt-hour) = energy consumed by 1 kW load for 1 hr = 3.6 MJ — your electricity bill 'unit'. metric HP = 735.5 W; imperial/mechanical HP = 745.7 W.

questions.stem: 0 KELVIN (absolute zero) corresponds to approximately what Celsius temperature?
questions.explanation: ABSOLUTE ZERO: the LOWEST possible temperature, where classical molecular motion CEASES (quantum zero-point energy remains). 0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F. TEMPERATURE SCALE CONVERSIONS: (1) K = °C + 273.15. (2) °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9. (3) °F = °C × 9/5 + 32. KEY POINTS: (a) Water FREEZES at 0°C = 273.15 K = 32°F (at 1 atm). (b) Water BOILS at 100°C = 373.15 K = 212°F (at 1 atm). (c) Human body temp ~37°C = 310.15 K = 98.6°F. (d) Room temp ~25°C = 298.15 K = 77°F. COLDEST NATURAL: Vostok, Antarctica −89.2°C (1983); LOWEST LAB temp: ~38 picokelvin (fraction above 0 K) achieved by Bose-Einstein condensates. DEEP SPACE cosmic microwave background temp ~2.725 K. 3rd LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: absolute zero is UNATTAINABLE — can approach it asymptotically. ABSOLUTE ZERO was extrapolated by WILLIAM THOMSON (Lord KELVIN) in 1848 — hence K scale. Earlier GAS-LAW data: Charles's Law (V∝T) linearly extrapolated to zero volume at −273°C. RANKINE scale (imperial absolute) rarely used. KELVIN is SI base unit → the only absolute temp in SI; NO 'degree' prefix (write 300 K, not 300°K). Redefined in 2019 via Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K. theoretical temperature at which particles have minimum vibrational (zero-point) motion.

questions.stem: The unit PARSEC (pc) used in astronomy equals approximately:

options.option_text: 1 light-year
3.26 LIGHT-YEARS
100 light-years
1 astronomical unit

questions.explanation: PARSEC (pc) — PAR(allax of one) SEC(ond of arc); the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of 1 ARCSECOND. 1 pc = 3.0857 × 10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.262 LIGHT-YEARS ≈ 206,265 AU. USE: professional astronomy — galaxies' distances measured in MEGAPARSECS (Mpc = 10⁶ pc) or KILOPARSECS (kpc = 10³ pc). EXAMPLES: (a) Proxima Centauri ≈ 1.301 pc (≈ 4.24 ly); (b) Milky Way radius ≈ 15-20 kpc; (c) Nearest major galaxy (Andromeda M31) ≈ 780 kpc; (d) Observable universe radius ≈ 14,000 Mpc. HUBBLE CONSTANT: ~70 km/s/Mpc. PARALLAX method: measure a star's apparent shift as Earth moves from one side of its orbit to the other (baseline = 2 AU). Tiny angular shift = 1/distance in pc. Only nearby stars (within ~300 pc) have measurable parallax from Earth; GAIA space telescope (ESA, 2013-launched) has mapped parallax for billions of stars to µarcsec precision — current gold standard for stellar distances. BEYOND parallax: STANDARD CANDLES (Cepheid variables' luminosity-period relation — Henrietta Leavitt, 1912; Type Ia supernovae); REDSHIFT (for distant galaxies, Hubble law). ASTRONOMICAL DISTANCES summary: AU (solar system) → ly or pc (stars) → kpc (galaxy) → Mpc (nearby galaxies) → Gpc (cosmological). distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond parallax; ≈ 3.086 × 10¹⁶ m.

questions.stem: Match the unit with the quantity measured: (1) TESLA (T); (2) WEBER (Wb); (3) HENRY (H); (4) FARAD (F).

options.option_text: Current, Voltage, Resistance, Power
Magnetic flux density; Magnetic flux; Inductance; Capacitance
Temperature, Radiation, Pressure, Frequency
Luminous intensity, Brightness, Resistance, Charge

questions.explanation: ELECTROMAGNETIC SI UNITS: (1) TESLA (T) — MAGNETIC FLUX DENSITY (Wb/m² = kg/(A·s²)); named after NIKOLA TESLA. Earth's magnetic field ~25-65 µT; fridge magnet ~5 mT; MRI machine ~1.5-7 T; LHC magnets ~8 T. (2) WEBER (Wb) — MAGNETIC FLUX (= V·s); named after WILHELM EDUARD WEBER. (3) HENRY (H) — INDUCTANCE (V·s/A = Wb/A); named after JOSEPH HENRY, American physicist who discovered self-inductance. (4) FARAD (F) — CAPACITANCE (C/V); named after MICHAEL FARADAY. Typical capacitors in microfarads (µF) or picofarads (pF); 1 F is very large (supercapacitors). OTHER ELECTRIC UNITS: OHM (Ω, Georg Ohm) = resistance; SIEMENS (S) = 1/Ω = conductance; COULOMB (C, Charles-Augustin de Coulomb) = A·s = charge; VOLT (V, Alessandro Volta) = J/C = potential. LUMINOUS UNITS: CANDELA (cd) = luminous intensity (base unit); LUMEN (lm) = luminous flux = cd·sr; LUX (lx) = lm/m² = illuminance. Reading a book needs ~400 lux; direct sunlight ~100,000 lux. RADIATION UNITS: BECQUEREL (Bq, Henri Becquerel) = 1 decay/sec (activity); CURIE (Ci, old unit) = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq; GRAY (Gy, Louis Harold Gray) = J/kg = absorbed dose; SIEVERT (Sv, Rolf Sievert) = J/kg = equivalent dose (biological effect); banana ~0.1 µSv; dental X-ray ~5 µSv; annual natural background ~3 mSv; lethal ~4 Sv.

questions.stem: The SI PREFIX for 10⁻¹² (one trillionth) is:

options.option_text: Nano (n)
PICO (p) — as in picofarad (pF), picometre (pm), picosecond (ps)
Micro (µ)
Femto (f)

questions.explanation: SI PREFIX TABLE (magnitude ↑ top, ↓ bottom): | 10²⁴ YOTTA (Y); 10²¹ ZETTA (Z); 10¹⁸ EXA (E); 10¹⁵ PETA (P); 10¹² TERA (T); 10⁹ GIGA (G); 10⁶ MEGA (M); 10³ KILO (k); 10² hecto (h); 10¹ deca (da); 10⁰ BASE UNIT; 10⁻¹ deci (d); 10⁻² centi (c); 10⁻³ MILLI (m); 10⁻⁶ MICRO (µ); 10⁻⁹ NANO (n); 10⁻¹² PICO (p); 10⁻¹⁵ FEMTO (f); 10⁻¹⁸ ATTO (a); 10⁻²¹ ZEPTO (z); 10⁻²⁴ YOCTO (y). 2022 addition (26th CGPM): RONTO (r, 10⁻²⁷), QUECTO (q, 10⁻³⁰), RONNA (R, 10²⁷), QUETTA (Q, 10³⁰). EXAMPLES: (a) PICOSECOND — time for light to travel 0.3 mm; laser pulse timescale. (b) PICOMETRE — atomic scale (H atom radius ~53 pm). (c) PICOFARAD — common capacitor value in electronics. FEMTOSECOND laser = 10⁻¹⁵ s — can photograph electrons in motion (Nobel Physics 2023 to Agostini, Krausz, L'Huillier). ATTOSECOND — 10⁻¹⁸ s, shorter than an electron's orbital period. NANOSECOND: light travels 30 cm in 1 ns — limits clock speed in CPUs. Human reaction time ~200 ms (200 million ns). 'RONNABYTE' + 'QUETTABYTE' = new large data units.

questions.stem: In the International System of Units (SI), 'radian' and 'steradian' are classified as which type of units?

options.option_text: Base units — fundamental quantities like mass and time
Supplementary units — for plane and solid angle measure
Derived units — expressed as products of base SI units
Coherent units — reserved for electromagnetic quantities

questions.explanation: B is correct. In the original SI framework, radian (plane angle) and steradian (solid angle) were designated 'supplementary units' — a special category separate from the 7 base units and derived units. Option A is wrong because the 7 base units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela) do not include radian or steradian. Option C is wrong because derived units are formed from base units by multiplication or division (e.g., Newton = kg·m·s⁻²), whereas radian and steradian are purely geometric ratios. Option D ('coherent units') is not a recognised SI classification.

questions.stem: The SI base unit used to quantify the 'amount of substance' in a chemical sample is the:

options.option_text: Mole, representing 6.022 × 10²³ constituent entities
Dalton, the unified atomic mass unit used in chemistry
Gram-equivalent, defined via normality in a solution
Faraday, representing one mole of electron charge units

questions.explanation: A is correct. The mole (mol) is the SI base unit for amount of substance, defined since 2019 as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (Avogadro's number). Option B (Dalton / unified atomic mass unit, u) is used to express atomic and molecular masses but is not an SI base unit. Option C (gram-equivalent) belongs to the older equivalent-weight system and is absent from modern SI. Option D (Faraday ≈ 96485 C/mol) is a unit of electric charge per mole of electrons — related to amount of substance but not the unit for it.

questions.stem: The dimensional formula [ML⁻¹T⁻²] corresponds to which of the following physical quantities?

options.option_text: Kinematic viscosity — SI unit is square metre per second
Surface tension — force per unit length along an interface
Pressure or mechanical stress — force per unit cross-section
Coefficient of viscosity — resistance to fluid flow (Pa·s)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Pressure = Force / Area = [MLT⁻²] / [L²] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²]. The same formula applies to mechanical stress, bulk modulus, and Young's modulus. Option A (kinematic viscosity ν = η/ρ) has dimensions [L²T⁻¹]. Option B (surface tension = F/l) has dimensions [MT⁻²]. Option D (coefficient of dynamic viscosity η) has dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻¹] — note the T exponent is −1, not −2, a very common confusion with pressure since both share the ML⁻¹ factor.

questions.stem: Which of the following physical quantities is truly dimensionless, with dimensional formula [M⁰L⁰T⁰]?

options.option_text: Angular velocity — angular displacement divided by time
Strain — ratio of change in length to the original length
Surface charge density — electric charge spread over area
Specific heat capacity — heat absorbed per kilogram per kelvin

questions.explanation: B is correct. Strain = ΔL / L — both numerator and denominator have dimension [L], so they cancel completely, giving [M⁰L⁰T⁰]. Option A (angular velocity ω = θ/t) has dimension [T⁻¹]; even though the radian is treated as dimensionless, ω still carries per-unit-time. Option C (surface charge density σ = Q/A) has dimensions [A·T·L⁻²]. Option D (specific heat c = Q/(m·ΔT)) has dimensions [L²T⁻²K⁻¹] — involving length, time, and temperature — definitely not dimensionless.

questions.stem: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the Weber (Wb). Which of the following correctly expresses one Weber in terms of other SI units?

options.option_text: Ampere per henry (A·H⁻¹) — inverting the inductance relation
Volt × second (V·s) — derived from Faraday's law of induction
Newton per square ampere (N·A⁻²) — from electromagnetic field terms
Tesla per square metre (T·m⁻²) — dividing instead of multiplying area

questions.explanation: B is correct. Faraday's law states EMF = −dΦ/dt, so Φ (Wb) = EMF × time = V·s. Equivalently, 1 Wb = 1 T·m² (flux = field × area). Option A is wrong: since inductance H = Wb/A, we get A/H = A²/Wb ≠ Wb. Option C: N/A² has dimensions [ML·T⁻²·A⁻²], which is the unit of magnetic permeability (H/m), not flux. Option D: T·m⁻² = (Wb/m²)·m⁻² = Wb·m⁻⁴ ≠ Wb — dividing by m² gives the magnetic field (Tesla), whereas multiplying by m² gives flux (Weber).

questions.stem: In the viscosity equation F = η·A·(dv/dx), where F is shear force, A is area, and dv/dx is velocity gradient, the dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity η is:

options.option_text: [ML⁻¹T⁻¹] — Newton-second per square metre, i.e., Pa·s
[ML⁻¹T⁻²] — same as pressure; confuses viscosity with stress
[MLT⁻²] — the dimension of force itself, not a transport property
[M⁰L²T⁻¹] — kinematic viscosity (ν = η/ρ), not dynamic η

questions.explanation: A is correct. Rearranging: η = F / (A · dv/dx). F → [MLT⁻²]; A → [L²]; dv/dx = (m/s)/m → [T⁻¹]. So η = [MLT⁻²] / ([L²][T⁻¹]) = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]. Option B ([ML⁻¹T⁻²]) is the dimension of pressure — the most common error since both share ML⁻¹ but pressure has T⁻² while dynamic viscosity has T⁻¹ (one fewer power of inverse time). Option D ([L²T⁻¹]) is kinematic viscosity ν = η/ρ, obtained by dividing η by density [ML⁻³] — a different quantity entirely. Option C simply equals the dimension of force, a structural error in applying the formula.

questions.stem: A physical quantity P = a²b³/√c. The percentage errors in measuring a, b, and c are 2%, 1%, and 4% respectively. The maximum percentage error in P is:

options.option_text: 7% — ignoring c's error contribution to the total budget
9% — applying power rule: 2×2% + 3×1% + ½×4% = 9%
11% — treating √c as c¹ and using the full 4% for c
12% — swapping the percentage errors of a and c inadvertently

questions.explanation: B is correct. Writing P = a²·b³·c^(−½), the maximum % error rule gives: |2|×(%Δa) + |3|×(%Δb) + |½|×(%Δc) = 2×2% + 3×1% + 0.5×4% = 4% + 3% + 2% = 9%. Option A (7%) arises from omitting c's term entirely (4+3=7). Option C (11%) is the most frequent student error — treating c^(1/2) as c¹, giving 2×2+3×1+1×4 = 4+3+4 = 11 (forgetting to halve the exponent for a square root). Option D (12%) results from swapping errors of a and c: 2×4% + 3×1% + ½×2% = 8+3+1 = 12.

questions.stem: Among the seven SI base units, which unit measures luminous intensity and carries the symbol 'cd'?

options.option_text: Lumen (lm) — measures total luminous flux emitted
Candela (cd) — measures luminous intensity of a source
Lux (lx) — measures illuminance on a receiving surface
Watt (W) — measures radiant power output of a source

questions.explanation: B is correct. The candela (cd) is the SI base unit of luminous intensity — it quantifies how bright a light source appears in a given direction. Lumen (lm) is a derived unit for total luminous flux; lux (lx) is illuminance (lm/m²); watt measures radiant power (not photometric). The candela is the only photometric quantity among the 7 SI base units, making it a frequent exam pick.

questions.stem: One standard atmosphere (atm), a widely referenced unit of pressure, is approximately equal to how many Pascals (Pa)?

options.option_text: 1.013 × 10⁴ Pa (ten thousand pascals approx.)
1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (one hundred thousand pascals approx.)
1.013 × 10³ Pa (one thousand pascals approx.)
1.013 × 10⁷ Pa (ten million pascals approx.)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 1 atm = 101,325 Pa ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. A common error is choosing 10⁴ Pa (option A), which is only one-tenth of an atmosphere. Option C (10³ Pa) corresponds roughly to 10 cm of water pressure. Since 1 Pa = 1 N/m², atmospheric pressure means about 100,000 newtons pressing on every square metre of surface — a useful intuition for exam problems.

questions.stem: The SI unit 'Henry' (H) measures which physical quantity, and after which scientist is it named?

options.option_text: Electric capacitance; named after British physicist James Henry
Electrical inductance; named after American physicist Joseph Henry
Magnetic flux density; named after Scottish physicist Joseph Henry
Electric conductance; named after Irish physicist William Henry

questions.explanation: B is correct. The henry (H) is the SI unit of electrical inductance — it measures a coil's opposition to changing current. Joseph Henry (1797–1878) was an American physicist who independently discovered electromagnetic induction around the same time as Faraday. Capacitance uses the farad (F); magnetic flux density uses the tesla (T); conductance uses the siemens (S). The nationality detail ('American') is a frequent exam twist.

questions.stem: The older unit of radioactivity, the 'Curie' (Ci), remains common in medical physics. How many Becquerel (Bq) equal approximately one Curie?

options.option_text: 3.7 × 10⁷ Bq (thirty-seven million disintegrations/s)
3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq (thirty-seven billion disintegrations/s)
3.7 × 10¹³ Bq (thirty-seven trillion disintegrations/s)
3.7 × 10⁴ Bq (thirty-seven thousand disintegrations/s)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 1 Curie = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq, defined from the activity of 1 gram of radium-226. The Becquerel (SI unit) equals exactly 1 nuclear decay per second, so 1 Ci represents 37 billion decays every second — an enormous rate. Option A (10⁷) is a common error where students misremember the exponent. Marie Curie's pioneering work on radium directly inspired this non-SI unit that still appears in clinical dosimetry.

questions.stem: The dimensional formula of coefficient of viscosity (η) is derived from η = (Force × distance) / (Area × velocity). Which expression is correct?

options.option_text: [ML⁻¹T⁻¹] — mass per length per time (SI unit: Pa·s)
[MLT⁻²] — identical dimensional formula as force in newtons
[ML²T⁻²] — identical dimensional formula as energy or work
[ML⁻¹T⁻²] — identical dimensional formula as pressure or stress

questions.explanation: A is correct. η = F·d / (A·v) = [MLT⁻²][L] / ([L²][LT⁻¹]) = [ML²T⁻²] / [L³T⁻¹] = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]. The SI unit is Pa·s (pascal-second). Option D ([ML⁻¹T⁻²]) is pressure/stress — the most tempting wrong answer since both involve force per area. The extra T⁻¹ in viscosity comes from dividing by velocity (speed has dimension [LT⁻¹]), giving one more negative power of T compared to pressure.

questions.stem: A student derives a formula whose result carries the dimensional formula [ML²T⁻³A⁻²]. Which physical quantity does this correspond to?

options.option_text: Electric capacitance in farads (charge stored per volt)
Electrical resistance in ohms (voltage per unit current)
Magnetic permeability in henrys per metre (H/m units)
Electric permittivity in farads per metre (F/m units)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Resistance R = V/I. Voltage V = Work/Charge = [ML²T⁻²]/[AT] = [ML²T⁻³A⁻¹]. So R = V/I = [ML²T⁻³A⁻¹]/[A] = [ML²T⁻³A⁻²]. Capacitance C = Q/V gives [M⁻¹L⁻²T⁴A²] — entirely different. Permeability is [MLT⁻²A⁻²]; permittivity is [M⁻¹L⁻³T⁴A²]. The signature of resistance is two negative powers of A (current appears in the denominator twice: once inside voltage and once as the divisor), which distinguishes it from all other electromagnetic quantities.

questions.stem: In the 2019 SI redefinition, the kilogram was decoupled from the Paris prototype artefact by fixing the exact value of which fundamental constant?

options.option_text: Avogadro constant Nₐ (fixed at 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ exactly)
Planck's constant h (fixed at 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s exactly)
Boltzmann constant k (fixed at 1.380 × 10⁻²³ J·K⁻¹ exactly)
Speed of light c (fixed at 2.998 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹ since 1983)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Since 2019, 1 kg is defined by fixing h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s exactly, realised experimentally via the Kibble (watt) balance. The old kg was a platinum-iridium cylinder in Sèvres, France — the sole SI unit still tied to a physical object until 2019. Each redefined unit maps to one constant: kelvin → Boltzmann constant k; mole → Avogadro constant Nₐ; ampere → elementary charge e; metre → speed of light c (since 1983). The Planck's constant → kilogram link is the most tested in competitive exams.
